presentation:
"{
  "Basic Information": "Female proband, born full term at 37th week, with a birth weight of 2 Kg and a head circumference of 32 cm. Parents are healthy and had a consanguineous marriage.",
  "Clinical Presentation": "The affected child has features typical of Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS) such as a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Additionally, she had right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly. Eye examination revealed hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other features include talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect, along with long hands and feet. She also had bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, and partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe. Sparse scalp hairs (alopecia) and prominent veins were noted. She was on a ventilator for the first few days after birth and received platelet transfusions on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.",
  "Physical Examination": "The affected child exhibited a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly were noted. Eye examination found hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other observations included talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect. Presence of long hands and feet, bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe, sparse scalp hairs (alopecia), and prominent veins were also recorded.",
  "Past Medical History": "Parents are healthy and did not reveal any disease phenotypes.",
  "Initial Test Results": "Platelet transfusions were given on the 5th and 7th postnatal days."
}"
most_likely_diagnosis: Ciliopathy with progeroid manifestations (Ciliopathy-progeroid overlap syndrome)
differential_diagnoses: Autosomal recessive disorder of DNA repair with progeroid features (e.g., Fanconi anemia-related, RECQL4, ERCC4)
Connective tissue or craniofacial disorder (e.g., Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome) with secondary anterior segment involvement
Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome with atypical ocular manifestations
recommended_tests: Whole exome sequencing with comprehensive analysis of ciliopathy (e.g., CEP120, IFT genes), progeroid (ZMPSTE24, LMNA, CENP), DNA repair (ERCC4, RECQL4), and connective tissue disorder genes (TGFBR1/2, FBN1, SKI)
Echocardiogram to assess for aortic root dilation and congenital heart disease
Complete ophthalmology evaluation with intraocular pressure measurement, gonioscopy, and lens examination
If WES negative, consider whole genome sequencing for non-coding variants
areas_of_disagreement: The genetics committee favors an autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder as the top hypothesis, while the pediatrics committee prioritizes a ciliopathy-progeroid overlap, and the ophthalmology committee suggests a connective tissue/craniofacial disorder or atypical Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome.
The presence of neonatal thrombocytopenia is highlighted by genetics as supporting a DNA repair disorder, but pediatrics and ophthalmology do not emphasize this feature.
Ophthalmology considers the ocular findings (glaucoma, ectopia lentis) atypical for classic Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch, whereas other committees integrate these as possible within a broader syndrome.

event_log.full_content:
Case presentation:
"{\n  \"Basic Information\": \"Female proband, born full term at 37th week, with a birth weight of 2 Kg and a head circumference of 32 cm. Parents are healthy and had a consanguineous marriage.\",\n  \"Clinical Presentation\": \"The affected child has features typical of Wiedemann\u2013Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS) such as a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Additionally, she had right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly. Eye examination revealed hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other features include talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect, along with long hands and feet. She also had bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, and partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe. Sparse scalp hairs (alopecia) and prominent veins were noted. She was on a ventilator for the first few days after birth and received platelet transfusions on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\",\n  \"Physical Examination\": \"The affected child exhibited a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly were noted. Eye examination found hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other observations included talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect. Presence of long hands and feet, bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe, sparse scalp hairs (alopecia), and prominent veins were also recorded.\",\n  \"Past Medical History\": \"Parents are healthy and did not reveal any disease phenotypes.\",\n  \"Initial Test Results\": \"Platelet transfusions were given on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\"\n}"

event_log.full_content:
Committee internal round-robin discussion.
Case presentation:
"{\n  \"Basic Information\": \"Female proband, born full term at 37th week, with a birth weight of 2 Kg and a head circumference of 32 cm. Parents are healthy and had a consanguineous marriage.\",\n  \"Clinical Presentation\": \"The affected child has features typical of Wiedemann\u2013Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS) such as a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Additionally, she had right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly. Eye examination revealed hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other features include talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect, along with long hands and feet. She also had bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, and partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe. Sparse scalp hairs (alopecia) and prominent veins were noted. She was on a ventilator for the first few days after birth and received platelet transfusions on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\",\n  \"Physical Examination\": \"The affected child exhibited a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly were noted. Eye examination found hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other observations included talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect. Presence of long hands and feet, bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe, sparse scalp hairs (alopecia), and prominent veins were also recorded.\",\n  \"Past Medical History\": \"Parents are healthy and did not reveal any disease phenotypes.\",\n  \"Initial Test Results\": \"Platelet transfusions were given on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\"\n}"

event_log.full_content:
**Neonatal specialist point:**

From a neonatal perspective, the requirement for ventilator support and platelet transfusions in the first week is a key red flag. Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome typically does **not** feature neonatal thrombocytopenia or respiratory distress necessitating ventilation. The presence of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, and complex ocular anomalies (glaucoma, ectopia lentis, hazy cornea) further deviates from classic WRS. Given consanguinity, an autosomal recessive multiple congenital anomaly syndrome is likely. I suspect a disorder involving either a ciliopathy (polydactyly + renal + cardiac + craniosynostosis) or a severe connective tissue/metabolic condition (lipodystrophy + ectopia lentis + thrombocytopenia). I would challenge over-interpreting the WRS-like features.

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome or genome sequencing, with rapid analysis for recessive causes of neonatal progeroid features plus craniosynostosis and thrombocytopenia (e.g., *FBN1* negative, but consider *ZMPSTE24*, *LMNA*, or ciliopathy genes such as *CENPF?*). Also consider a thrombocytopenia workup (e.g., TAR syndrome but radius normal?). Missing piece: platelet count details and bone marrow evaluation.

event_log.full_content:
**Growth/development specialist point:**

The intrauterine growth restriction (birth weight 2 kg at 37 weeks, <3rd percentile) with relative macrocephaly (head circumference 32 cm, ~10th–25th percentile) and severe congenital lipodystrophy creates a striking disproportionate growth pattern. In classic Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome, birth weight is usually normal to low-normal, and head circumference is typically above the 90th percentile, but the degree of IUGR here is more pronounced than commonly described. The combination of IUGR + lipodystrophy + multiple congenital anomalies (craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, complex eye defects, cardiac, renal) and neonatal thrombocytopenia is not a recognized feature of WRS. This pattern is more consistent with a severe autosomal recessive ciliopathy or a progeroid syndrome with a broader multi-organ involvement (e.g., *CENPF*-related ciliopathy, which can include IUGR, craniosynostosis, polydactyly, renal anomalies, and lipodystrophy). 

**Suspected direction:** A recessive ciliopathy or severe progeroid syndrome with craniosynostosis and polydactyly component.

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome sequencing with trio analysis, prioritizing ciliopathy and progeroid gene panels.

**Uncertainty:** Lack of developmental milestone data and post-natal growth trajectory is a missing piece to confirm the progressive nature of lipodystrophy.

event_log.full_content:
**Pediatric complexity reviewer point:**  
The co-occurrence of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, and bilateral hydronephrosis is a classic ciliopathy triad. However, the additional congenital lipodystrophy, ectopia lentis, and neonatal thrombocytopenia are not typical for most known ciliopathies and suggest a broader pathogenic mechanism—possibly a disorder affecting both ciliary function and nuclear envelope integrity (e.g., *ZMPSTE24* or *LMNA* progeroid syndromes, but these lack polydactyly). I suspect an ultra-rare recessive syndrome bridging ciliopathy and progeroid features, such as a *CENPF*-related disorder (which can include craniosynostosis, polydactyly, IUGR, renal anomalies, and occasional lipodystrophy) or a novel entity.  

**Strongest pediatric red flag against WRS:**  
Polydactyly and syndactyly are not features of Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome. Craniosynostosis is also atypical.  

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome or genome sequencing with trio analysis, prioritizing ciliopathy and progeroid gene panels, including *CENPF*, *ZMPSTE24*, *LMNA*, and *IFT* genes.  

**Limitation:** Absence of brain imaging (e.g., ventriculomegaly, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia) and platelet count/bone marrow details limits assessment of syndromic severity and ciliopathy involvement.

event_log.short_content_summary: As a dysmorphology specialist, I note that the combination of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, and congenital heart disease, together with progeroid f
event_log.full_content: As a dysmorphology specialist, I note that the combination of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, and congenital heart disease, together with progeroid features like lipodystrophy and sparse hair, is not typical for classic Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome. The presence of ectopia lentis and glaucoma further widens the differential. This pattern suggests a possible disorder of DNA repair or a ciliopathy with overlapping progeroid manifestations, especially given the consanguinity. I would direct genetic testing toward whole exome sequencing with attention to genes involved in nucleotide excision repair or centrosome function, as a single-gene recessive syndrome best explains the multi-system involvement. A limitation is the lack of reported metabolic or skeletal survey details that might further differentiate syndromes.

event_log.short_content_summary: As a variant interpretation specialist, I support the dysmorphology specialist's direction toward an autosomal recessive single-gene syndrome given consanguinit
event_log.full_content: As a variant interpretation specialist, I support the dysmorphology specialist's direction toward an autosomal recessive single-gene syndrome given consanguinity. The combination of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, congenital heart disease, progeroid features (lipodystrophy, alopecia), and ectopia lentis is highly distinctive and narrows the differential. I would prioritize whole exome sequencing with analysis focused on biallelic variants in genes associated with DNA repair (e.g., ERCC4, RECQL4) and ciliary/centrosome function (e.g., CEP120, IFT genes), as both categories can present with overlapping features such as craniosynostosis, polydactyly, and progeroid changes. The platelet transfusion history may hint at an associated bone marrow component occasionally seen in some DNA repair disorders, which could further guide filtering. A limitation is the lack of reported metabolic screening or skeletal survey to better discriminate between these categories, but the phenotype is sufficiently complex to make exome sequencing the most efficient first-line test for a likely novel or rare recessive diagnosis.

event_log.short_content_summary: As the family history analyst, I highlight that the consanguineous union (parents are first cousins or closer, though degree not specified) and absence of other
event_log.full_content: As the family history analyst, I highlight that the consanguineous union (parents are first cousins or closer, though degree not specified) and absence of other affected family members strongly support an autosomal recessive etiology. This pattern, combined with the complex multisystem involvement, is consistent with a rare recessive syndrome. The history of platelet transfusions in the neonatal period may indicate a transient bone marrow component sometimes seen in certain recessive DNA repair disorders (e.g., Fanconi anemia-related genes) or could be incidental. I recommend prioritizing whole exome sequencing with additional focus on runs of homozygosity to efficiently identify biallelic variants in recessive genes, given that consanguinity increases the likelihood of a homozygous mutation. A limitation is that without known ethnic background or degree of consanguinity, we cannot estimate the genetic distance, but this does not detract from the overall approach.

event_log.short_content_summary: From an ophthalmology perspective, the key ocular findings are congenital glaucoma, ectopia lentis, proptosis, and right-sided facial palsy with inability to cl
event_log.full_content: From an ophthalmology perspective, the key ocular findings are congenital glaucoma, ectopia lentis, proptosis, and right-sided facial palsy with inability to close the eye leading to exposure keratopathy and hazy cornea. This combination is atypical for classic Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS), where proptosis may occur but glaucoma and ectopia lentis are not characteristic features. The presence of both ectopia lentis and congenital glaucoma in a neonate with craniosynostosis and proptosis raises the possibility of a connective tissue or craniofacial disorder with secondary anterior segment dysgenesis. Differential considerations include a disorder of peroxisomal biogenesis (e.g., Zellweger spectrum), which can present with craniofacial anomalies, glaucoma, ectopia lentis, and hypotonia, but does not typically include lipodystrophy or polydactyly. Alternatively, a severe neonatal progeroid syndrome with expanded phenotype cannot be excluded. I suggest measuring very long-chain fatty acids and performing transferrin isoelectric focusing to evaluate for peroxisomal and glycosylation disorders. Additionally, high-resolution ocular ultrasound or anterior segment OCT would help document angle anatomy and lens position, and provide evidence for or against a primary developmental glaucoma versus secondary lens-related elevation.

"{\n  \"Basic Information\": \"Female proband, born full term at 37th week, with a birth weight of 2 Kg and a head circumference of 32 cm. Other features include talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect, along with long hands and feet. She also had bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, and partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe. Sparse scalp hairs (alopecia) and prominent veins were noted. She was on a ventilator for the first few days after birth and received platelet transfusions on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\",\n  \"Physical Examination\": \"The affected child exhibited a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly were noted. Eye examination found hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other observations included talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect. Presence of long hands and feet, bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe, sparse scalp hairs (alopecia), and prominent veins were also recorded.\",\n  \"Past Medical History\": \"Parents are healthy and did not reveal any disease phenotypes.\",\n  \"Initial Test Results\": \"Platelet transfusions were given on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\"\n}"

Parents are healthy and had a consanguineous marriage.\",\n  \"Clinical Presentation\": \"The affected child has features typical of Wiedemann\u2013Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS) such as a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Other features include talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect, along with long hands and feet. She also had bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, and partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe. Sparse scalp hairs (alopecia) and prominent veins were noted. She was on a ventilator for the first few days after birth and received platelet transfusions on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\",\n  \"Physical Examination\": \"The affected child exhibited a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly were noted. Eye examination found hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other observations included talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect. Presence of long hands and feet, bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe, sparse scalp hairs (alopecia), and prominent veins were also recorded.\",\n  \"Past Medical History\": \"Parents are healthy and did not reveal any disease phenotypes.\",\n  \"Initial Test Results\": \"Platelet transfusions were given on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\"\n}"

**Neonatal specialist point:**

From a neonatal perspective, the requirement for ventilator support and platelet transfusions in the first week is a key red flag. Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome typically does **not** feature neonatal thrombocytopenia or respiratory distress necessitating ventilation. The presence of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, and complex ocular anomalies (glaucoma, ectopia lentis, hazy cornea) further deviates from classic WRS. Given consanguinity, an autosomal recessive multiple congenital anomaly syndrome is likely. I suspect a disorder involving either a ciliopathy (polydactyly + renal + cardiac + craniosynostosis) or a severe connective tissue/metabolic condition (lipodystrophy + ectopia lentis + thrombocytopenia). I would challenge over-interpreting the WRS-like features.

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome or genome sequencing, with rapid analysis for recessive causes of neonatal progeroid features plus craniosynostosis and thrombocytopenia (e.g., *FBN1* negative, but consider *ZMPSTE24*, *LMNA*, or ciliopathy genes such as *CENPF?*). Also consider a thrombocytopenia workup (e.g., TAR syndrome but radius normal?). Missing piece: platelet count details and bone marrow evaluation.

**Growth/development specialist point:**

The intrauterine growth restriction (birth weight 2 kg at 37 weeks, <3rd percentile) with relative macrocephaly (head circumference 32 cm, ~10th–25th percentile) and severe congenital lipodystrophy creates a striking disproportionate growth pattern. In classic Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome, birth weight is usually normal to low-normal, and head circumference is typically above the 90th percentile, but the degree of IUGR here is more pronounced than commonly described. The combination of IUGR + lipodystrophy + multiple congenital anomalies (craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, complex eye defects, cardiac, renal) and neonatal thrombocytopenia is not a recognized feature of WRS. This pattern is more consistent with a severe autosomal recessive ciliopathy or a progeroid syndrome with a broader multi-organ involvement (e.g., *CENPF*-related ciliopathy, which can include IUGR, craniosynostosis, polydactyly, renal anomalies, and lipodystrophy). 

**Suspected direction:** A recessive ciliopathy or severe progeroid syndrome with craniosynostosis and polydactyly component.

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome sequencing with trio analysis, prioritizing ciliopathy and progeroid gene panels.

**Uncertainty:** Lack of developmental milestone data and post-natal growth trajectory is a missing piece to confirm the progressive nature of lipodystrophy.

**Pediatric complexity reviewer point:**  
The co-occurrence of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, and bilateral hydronephrosis is a classic ciliopathy triad. However, the additional congenital lipodystrophy, ectopia lentis, and neonatal thrombocytopenia are not typical for most known ciliopathies and suggest a broader pathogenic mechanism—possibly a disorder affecting both ciliary function and nuclear envelope integrity (e.g., *ZMPSTE24* or *LMNA* progeroid syndromes, but these lack polydactyly). I suspect an ultra-rare recessive syndrome bridging ciliopathy and progeroid features, such as a *CENPF*-related disorder (which can include craniosynostosis, polydactyly, IUGR, renal anomalies, and occasional lipodystrophy) or a novel entity.  

**Strongest pediatric red flag against WRS:**  
Polydactyly and syndactyly are not features of Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome. Craniosynostosis is also atypical.  

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome or genome sequencing with trio analysis, prioritizing ciliopathy and progeroid gene panels, including *CENPF*, *ZMPSTE24*, *LMNA*, and *IFT* genes.  

**Limitation:** Absence of brain imaging (e.g., ventriculomegaly, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia) and platelet count/bone marrow details limits assessment of syndromic severity and ciliopathy involvement.

As a dysmorphology specialist, I note that the combination of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, and congenital heart disease, together with progeroid features like lipodystrophy and sparse hair, is not typical for classic Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome. The presence of ectopia lentis and glaucoma further widens the differential. This pattern suggests a possible disorder of DNA repair or a ciliopathy with overlapping progeroid manifestations, especially given the consanguinity. I would direct genetic testing toward whole exome sequencing with attention to genes involved in nucleotide excision repair or centrosome function, as a single-gene recessive syndrome best explains the multi-system involvement. A limitation is the lack of reported metabolic or skeletal survey details that might further differentiate syndromes.

As a variant interpretation specialist, I support the dysmorphology specialist's direction toward an autosomal recessive single-gene syndrome given consanguinity. The combination of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, congenital heart disease, progeroid features (lipodystrophy, alopecia), and ectopia lentis is highly distinctive and narrows the differential. I would prioritize whole exome sequencing with analysis focused on biallelic variants in genes associated with DNA repair (e.g., ERCC4, RECQL4) and ciliary/centrosome function (e.g., CEP120, IFT genes), as both categories can present with overlapping features such as craniosynostosis, polydactyly, and progeroid changes. The platelet transfusion history may hint at an associated bone marrow component occasionally seen in some DNA repair disorders, which could further guide filtering. A limitation is the lack of reported metabolic screening or skeletal survey to better discriminate between these categories, but the phenotype is sufficiently complex to make exome sequencing the most efficient first-line test for a likely novel or rare recessive diagnosis.

As the family history analyst, I highlight that the consanguineous union (parents are first cousins or closer, though degree not specified) and absence of other affected family members strongly support an autosomal recessive etiology. This pattern, combined with the complex multisystem involvement, is consistent with a rare recessive syndrome. The history of platelet transfusions in the neonatal period may indicate a transient bone marrow component sometimes seen in certain recessive DNA repair disorders (e.g., Fanconi anemia-related genes) or could be incidental. I recommend prioritizing whole exome sequencing with additional focus on runs of homozygosity to efficiently identify biallelic variants in recessive genes, given that consanguinity increases the likelihood of a homozygous mutation. A limitation is that without known ethnic background or degree of consanguinity, we cannot estimate the genetic distance, but this does not detract from the overall approach.

From an ophthalmology perspective, the key ocular findings are congenital glaucoma, ectopia lentis, proptosis, and right-sided facial palsy with inability to close the eye leading to exposure keratopathy and hazy cornea. This combination is atypical for classic Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS), where proptosis may occur but glaucoma and ectopia lentis are not characteristic features. The presence of both ectopia lentis and congenital glaucoma in a neonate with craniosynostosis and proptosis raises the possibility of a connective tissue or craniofacial disorder with secondary anterior segment dysgenesis. Differential considerations include a disorder of peroxisomal biogenesis (e.g., Zellweger spectrum), which can present with craniofacial anomalies, glaucoma, ectopia lentis, and hypotonia, but does not typically include lipodystrophy or polydactyly. Alternatively, a severe neonatal progeroid syndrome with expanded phenotype cannot be excluded. I suggest measuring very long-chain fatty acids and performing transferrin isoelectric focusing to evaluate for peroxisomal and glycosylation disorders. Additionally, high-resolution ocular ultrasound or anterior segment OCT would help document angle anatomy and lens position, and provide evidence for or against a primary developmental glaucoma versus secondary lens-related elevation.

event_log.full_content:
Case presentation:
"{\n  \"Basic Information\": \"Female proband, born full term at 37th week, with a birth weight of 2 Kg and a head circumference of 32 cm. Parents are healthy and had a consanguineous marriage.\",\n  \"Clinical Presentation\": \"The affected child has features typical of Wiedemann\u2013Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS) such as a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Additionally, she had right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly. Eye examination revealed hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other features include talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect, along with long hands and feet. She also had bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, and partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe. Sparse scalp hairs (alopecia) and prominent veins were noted. She was on a ventilator for the first few days after birth and received platelet transfusions on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\",\n  \"Physical Examination\": \"The affected child exhibited a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly were noted. Eye examination found hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other observations included talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect. Presence of long hands and feet, bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe, sparse scalp hairs (alopecia), and prominent veins were also recorded.\",\n  \"Past Medical History\": \"Parents are healthy and did not reveal any disease phenotypes.\",\n  \"Initial Test Results\": \"Platelet transfusions were given on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\"\n}"

event_log.full_content:
Committee internal round-robin discussion.
Case presentation:
"{\n  \"Basic Information\": \"Female proband, born full term at 37th week, with a birth weight of 2 Kg and a head circumference of 32 cm. Parents are healthy and had a consanguineous marriage.\",\n  \"Clinical Presentation\": \"The affected child has features typical of Wiedemann\u2013Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS) such as a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Additionally, she had right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly. Eye examination revealed hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other features include talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect, along with long hands and feet. She also had bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, and partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe. Sparse scalp hairs (alopecia) and prominent veins were noted. She was on a ventilator for the first few days after birth and received platelet transfusions on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\",\n  \"Physical Examination\": \"The affected child exhibited a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly were noted. Eye examination found hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other observations included talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect. Presence of long hands and feet, bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe, sparse scalp hairs (alopecia), and prominent veins were also recorded.\",\n  \"Past Medical History\": \"Parents are healthy and did not reveal any disease phenotypes.\",\n  \"Initial Test Results\": \"Platelet transfusions were given on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\"\n}"

event_log.full_content:
**Neonatal specialist point:**

From a neonatal perspective, the requirement for ventilator support and platelet transfusions in the first week is a key red flag. Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome typically does **not** feature neonatal thrombocytopenia or respiratory distress necessitating ventilation. The presence of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, and complex ocular anomalies (glaucoma, ectopia lentis, hazy cornea) further deviates from classic WRS. Given consanguinity, an autosomal recessive multiple congenital anomaly syndrome is likely. I suspect a disorder involving either a ciliopathy (polydactyly + renal + cardiac + craniosynostosis) or a severe connective tissue/metabolic condition (lipodystrophy + ectopia lentis + thrombocytopenia). I would challenge over-interpreting the WRS-like features.

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome or genome sequencing, with rapid analysis for recessive causes of neonatal progeroid features plus craniosynostosis and thrombocytopenia (e.g., *FBN1* negative, but consider *ZMPSTE24*, *LMNA*, or ciliopathy genes such as *CENPF?*). Also consider a thrombocytopenia workup (e.g., TAR syndrome but radius normal?). Missing piece: platelet count details and bone marrow evaluation.

event_log.full_content:
**Growth/development specialist point:**

The intrauterine growth restriction (birth weight 2 kg at 37 weeks, <3rd percentile) with relative macrocephaly (head circumference 32 cm, ~10th–25th percentile) and severe congenital lipodystrophy creates a striking disproportionate growth pattern. In classic Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome, birth weight is usually normal to low-normal, and head circumference is typically above the 90th percentile, but the degree of IUGR here is more pronounced than commonly described. The combination of IUGR + lipodystrophy + multiple congenital anomalies (craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, complex eye defects, cardiac, renal) and neonatal thrombocytopenia is not a recognized feature of WRS. This pattern is more consistent with a severe autosomal recessive ciliopathy or a progeroid syndrome with a broader multi-organ involvement (e.g., *CENPF*-related ciliopathy, which can include IUGR, craniosynostosis, polydactyly, renal anomalies, and lipodystrophy). 

**Suspected direction:** A recessive ciliopathy or severe progeroid syndrome with craniosynostosis and polydactyly component.

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome sequencing with trio analysis, prioritizing ciliopathy and progeroid gene panels.

**Uncertainty:** Lack of developmental milestone data and post-natal growth trajectory is a missing piece to confirm the progressive nature of lipodystrophy.

event_log.full_content:
**Pediatric complexity reviewer point:**  
The co-occurrence of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, and bilateral hydronephrosis is a classic ciliopathy triad. However, the additional congenital lipodystrophy, ectopia lentis, and neonatal thrombocytopenia are not typical for most known ciliopathies and suggest a broader pathogenic mechanism—possibly a disorder affecting both ciliary function and nuclear envelope integrity (e.g., *ZMPSTE24* or *LMNA* progeroid syndromes, but these lack polydactyly). I suspect an ultra-rare recessive syndrome bridging ciliopathy and progeroid features, such as a *CENPF*-related disorder (which can include craniosynostosis, polydactyly, IUGR, renal anomalies, and occasional lipodystrophy) or a novel entity.  

**Strongest pediatric red flag against WRS:**  
Polydactyly and syndactyly are not features of Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome. Craniosynostosis is also atypical.  

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome or genome sequencing with trio analysis, prioritizing ciliopathy and progeroid gene panels, including *CENPF*, *ZMPSTE24*, *LMNA*, and *IFT* genes.  

**Limitation:** Absence of brain imaging (e.g., ventriculomegaly, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia) and platelet count/bone marrow details limits assessment of syndromic severity and ciliopathy involvement.

event_log.short_content_summary: As a dysmorphology specialist, I note that the combination of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, and congenital heart disease, together with progeroid f
event_log.full_content: As a dysmorphology specialist, I note that the combination of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, and congenital heart disease, together with progeroid features like lipodystrophy and sparse hair, is not typical for classic Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome. The presence of ectopia lentis and glaucoma further widens the differential. This pattern suggests a possible disorder of DNA repair or a ciliopathy with overlapping progeroid manifestations, especially given the consanguinity. I would direct genetic testing toward whole exome sequencing with attention to genes involved in nucleotide excision repair or centrosome function, as a single-gene recessive syndrome best explains the multi-system involvement. A limitation is the lack of reported metabolic or skeletal survey details that might further differentiate syndromes.

event_log.short_content_summary: As a variant interpretation specialist, I support the dysmorphology specialist's direction toward an autosomal recessive single-gene syndrome given consanguinit
event_log.full_content: As a variant interpretation specialist, I support the dysmorphology specialist's direction toward an autosomal recessive single-gene syndrome given consanguinity. The combination of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, congenital heart disease, progeroid features (lipodystrophy, alopecia), and ectopia lentis is highly distinctive and narrows the differential. I would prioritize whole exome sequencing with analysis focused on biallelic variants in genes associated with DNA repair (e.g., ERCC4, RECQL4) and ciliary/centrosome function (e.g., CEP120, IFT genes), as both categories can present with overlapping features such as craniosynostosis, polydactyly, and progeroid changes. The platelet transfusion history may hint at an associated bone marrow component occasionally seen in some DNA repair disorders, which could further guide filtering. A limitation is the lack of reported metabolic screening or skeletal survey to better discriminate between these categories, but the phenotype is sufficiently complex to make exome sequencing the most efficient first-line test for a likely novel or rare recessive diagnosis.

event_log.short_content_summary: As the family history analyst, I highlight that the consanguineous union (parents are first cousins or closer, though degree not specified) and absence of other
event_log.full_content: As the family history analyst, I highlight that the consanguineous union (parents are first cousins or closer, though degree not specified) and absence of other affected family members strongly support an autosomal recessive etiology. This pattern, combined with the complex multisystem involvement, is consistent with a rare recessive syndrome. The history of platelet transfusions in the neonatal period may indicate a transient bone marrow component sometimes seen in certain recessive DNA repair disorders (e.g., Fanconi anemia-related genes) or could be incidental. I recommend prioritizing whole exome sequencing with additional focus on runs of homozygosity to efficiently identify biallelic variants in recessive genes, given that consanguinity increases the likelihood of a homozygous mutation. A limitation is that without known ethnic background or degree of consanguinity, we cannot estimate the genetic distance, but this does not detract from the overall approach.

event_log.short_content_summary: From an ophthalmology perspective, the key ocular findings are congenital glaucoma, ectopia lentis, proptosis, and right-sided facial palsy with inability to cl
event_log.full_content: From an ophthalmology perspective, the key ocular findings are congenital glaucoma, ectopia lentis, proptosis, and right-sided facial palsy with inability to close the eye leading to exposure keratopathy and hazy cornea. This combination is atypical for classic Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS), where proptosis may occur but glaucoma and ectopia lentis are not characteristic features. The presence of both ectopia lentis and congenital glaucoma in a neonate with craniosynostosis and proptosis raises the possibility of a connective tissue or craniofacial disorder with secondary anterior segment dysgenesis. Differential considerations include a disorder of peroxisomal biogenesis (e.g., Zellweger spectrum), which can present with craniofacial anomalies, glaucoma, ectopia lentis, and hypotonia, but does not typically include lipodystrophy or polydactyly. Alternatively, a severe neonatal progeroid syndrome with expanded phenotype cannot be excluded. I suggest measuring very long-chain fatty acids and performing transferrin isoelectric focusing to evaluate for peroxisomal and glycosylation disorders. Additionally, high-resolution ocular ultrasound or anterior segment OCT would help document angle anatomy and lens position, and provide evidence for or against a primary developmental glaucoma versus secondary lens-related elevation.

event_log.full_content:
Committee: ophthalmology
Case presentation:
"{\n  \"Basic Information\": \"Female proband, born full term at 37th week, with a birth weight of 2 Kg and a head circumference of 32 cm. Parents are healthy and had a consanguineous marriage.\",\n  \"Clinical Presentation\": \"The affected child has features typical of Wiedemann\u2013Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS) such as a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Additionally, she had right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly. Eye examination revealed hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other features include talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect, along with long hands and feet. She also had bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, and partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe. Sparse scalp hairs (alopecia) and prominent veins were noted. She was on a ventilator for the first few days after birth and received platelet transfusions on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\",\n  \"Physical Examination\": \"The affected child exhibited a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly were noted. Eye examination found hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other observations included talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect. Presence of long hands and feet, bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe, sparse scalp hairs (alopecia), and prominent veins were also recorded.\",\n  \"Past Medical History\": \"Parents are healthy and did not reveal any disease phenotypes.\",\n  \"Initial Test Results\": \"Platelet transfusions were given on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\"\n}"

    "The presence of neonatal thrombocytopenia is highlighted by genetics as supporting a DNA repair disorder, but pediatrics and ophthalmology do not emphasize this feature.",
    "Ophthalmology considers the ocular findings (glaucoma, ectopia lentis) atypical for classic Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch, whereas other committees integrate these as possible within a broader syndrome."
  ],

Parents are healthy and had a consanguineous marriage.\",\n  \"Clinical Presentation\": \"The affected child has features typical of Wiedemann\u2013Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS) such as a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Additionally, she had right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly. Eye examination revealed hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other features include talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect, along with long hands and feet. She also had bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, and partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe. Sparse scalp hairs (alopecia) and prominent veins were noted. She was on a ventilator for the first few days after birth and received platelet transfusions on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\",\n  \"Physical Examination\": \"The affected child exhibited a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly were noted. Eye examination found hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other observations included talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect. Presence of long hands and feet, bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe, sparse scalp hairs (alopecia), and prominent veins were also recorded.\",\n  \"Past Medical History\": \"Parents are healthy and did not reveal any disease phenotypes.\",\n  \"Initial Test Results\": \"Platelet transfusions were given on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\"\n}"

"{\n  \"Basic Information\": \"Female proband, born full term at 37th week, with a birth weight of 2 Kg and a head circumference of 32 cm. Parents are healthy and had a consanguineous marriage.\",\n  \"Clinical Presentation\": \"The affected child has features typical of Wiedemann\u2013Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS) such as a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Additionally, she had right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly. Eye examination revealed hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other features include talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect, along with long hands and feet. She also had bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, and partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe. Sparse scalp hairs (alopecia) and prominent veins were noted. She was on a ventilator for the first few days after birth and received platelet transfusions on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\",\n  \"Physical Examination\": \"The affected child exhibited a large head, prominent forehead, beaked nose, craniofacial disproportion, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and rigid joints. Right-sided facial palsy, craniosynostosis, and scaphocephaly were noted. Eye examination found hazy cornea, inability to close right eye, glaucoma, proptosis, and ectopia lentis. Other observations included talipes calcaneovalgus, bilateral hydronephrosis, and ventricular septal defect. Presence of long hands and feet, bilateral polydactyly of hands, generalized lipodystrophy, partial syndactyly in the 2nd and 3rd toe, sparse scalp hairs (alopecia), and prominent veins were also recorded.\",\n  \"Past Medical History\": \"Parents are healthy and did not reveal any disease phenotypes.\",\n  \"Initial Test Results\": \"Platelet transfusions were given on the 5th and 7th postnatal days.\"\n}"

Do not provide treatment or management advice.

**Neonatal specialist point:**

From a neonatal perspective, the requirement for ventilator support and platelet transfusions in the first week is a key red flag. Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome typically does **not** feature neonatal thrombocytopenia or respiratory distress necessitating ventilation. The presence of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, and complex ocular anomalies (glaucoma, ectopia lentis, hazy cornea) further deviates from classic WRS. Given consanguinity, an autosomal recessive multiple congenital anomaly syndrome is likely. I suspect a disorder involving either a ciliopathy (polydactyly + renal + cardiac + craniosynostosis) or a severe connective tissue/metabolic condition (lipodystrophy + ectopia lentis + thrombocytopenia). I would challenge over-interpreting the WRS-like features.

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome or genome sequencing, with rapid analysis for recessive causes of neonatal progeroid features plus craniosynostosis and thrombocytopenia (e.g., *FBN1* negative, but consider *ZMPSTE24*, *LMNA*, or ciliopathy genes such as *CENPF?*). Also consider a thrombocytopenia workup (e.g., TAR syndrome but radius normal?). Missing piece: platelet count details and bone marrow evaluation.

**Growth/development specialist point:**

The intrauterine growth restriction (birth weight 2 kg at 37 weeks, <3rd percentile) with relative macrocephaly (head circumference 32 cm, ~10th–25th percentile) and severe congenital lipodystrophy creates a striking disproportionate growth pattern. In classic Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome, birth weight is usually normal to low-normal, and head circumference is typically above the 90th percentile, but the degree of IUGR here is more pronounced than commonly described. The combination of IUGR + lipodystrophy + multiple congenital anomalies (craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, complex eye defects, cardiac, renal) and neonatal thrombocytopenia is not a recognized feature of WRS. This pattern is more consistent with a severe autosomal recessive ciliopathy or a progeroid syndrome with a broader multi-organ involvement (e.g., *CENPF*-related ciliopathy, which can include IUGR, craniosynostosis, polydactyly, renal anomalies, and lipodystrophy). 

**Suspected direction:** A recessive ciliopathy or severe progeroid syndrome with craniosynostosis and polydactyly component.

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome sequencing with trio analysis, prioritizing ciliopathy and progeroid gene panels.

**Uncertainty:** Lack of developmental milestone data and post-natal growth trajectory is a missing piece to confirm the progressive nature of lipodystrophy.

**Pediatric complexity reviewer point:**  
The co-occurrence of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, and bilateral hydronephrosis is a classic ciliopathy triad. However, the additional congenital lipodystrophy, ectopia lentis, and neonatal thrombocytopenia are not typical for most known ciliopathies and suggest a broader pathogenic mechanism—possibly a disorder affecting both ciliary function and nuclear envelope integrity (e.g., *ZMPSTE24* or *LMNA* progeroid syndromes, but these lack polydactyly). I suspect an ultra-rare recessive syndrome bridging ciliopathy and progeroid features, such as a *CENPF*-related disorder (which can include craniosynostosis, polydactyly, IUGR, renal anomalies, and occasional lipodystrophy) or a novel entity.  

**Strongest pediatric red flag against WRS:**  
Polydactyly and syndactyly are not features of Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome. Craniosynostosis is also atypical.  

**Highest-yield test:** Whole-exome or genome sequencing with trio analysis, prioritizing ciliopathy and progeroid gene panels, including *CENPF*, *ZMPSTE24*, *LMNA*, and *IFT* genes.  

**Limitation:** Absence of brain imaging (e.g., ventriculomegaly, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia) and platelet count/bone marrow details limits assessment of syndromic severity and ciliopathy involvement.

As a dysmorphology specialist, I note that the combination of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, and congenital heart disease, together with progeroid features like lipodystrophy and sparse hair, is not typical for classic Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome. The presence of ectopia lentis and glaucoma further widens the differential. This pattern suggests a possible disorder of DNA repair or a ciliopathy with overlapping progeroid manifestations, especially given the consanguinity. I would direct genetic testing toward whole exome sequencing with attention to genes involved in nucleotide excision repair or centrosome function, as a single-gene recessive syndrome best explains the multi-system involvement. A limitation is the lack of reported metabolic or skeletal survey details that might further differentiate syndromes.

As a variant interpretation specialist, I support the dysmorphology specialist's direction toward an autosomal recessive single-gene syndrome given consanguinity. The combination of craniosynostosis, polydactyly, syndactyly, congenital heart disease, progeroid features (lipodystrophy, alopecia), and ectopia lentis is highly distinctive and narrows the differential. I would prioritize whole exome sequencing with analysis focused on biallelic variants in genes associated with DNA repair (e.g., ERCC4, RECQL4) and ciliary/centrosome function (e.g., CEP120, IFT genes), as both categories can present with overlapping features such as craniosynostosis, polydactyly, and progeroid changes. The platelet transfusion history may hint at an associated bone marrow component occasionally seen in some DNA repair disorders, which could further guide filtering. A limitation is the lack of reported metabolic screening or skeletal survey to better discriminate between these categories, but the phenotype is sufficiently complex to make exome sequencing the most efficient first-line test for a likely novel or rare recessive diagnosis.

As the family history analyst, I highlight that the consanguineous union (parents are first cousins or closer, though degree not specified) and absence of other affected family members strongly support an autosomal recessive etiology. This pattern, combined with the complex multisystem involvement, is consistent with a rare recessive syndrome. The history of platelet transfusions in the neonatal period may indicate a transient bone marrow component sometimes seen in certain recessive DNA repair disorders (e.g., Fanconi anemia-related genes) or could be incidental. I recommend prioritizing whole exome sequencing with additional focus on runs of homozygosity to efficiently identify biallelic variants in recessive genes, given that consanguinity increases the likelihood of a homozygous mutation. A limitation is that without known ethnic background or degree of consanguinity, we cannot estimate the genetic distance, but this does not detract from the overall approach.

From an ophthalmology perspective, the key ocular findings are congenital glaucoma, ectopia lentis, proptosis, and right-sided facial palsy with inability to close the eye leading to exposure keratopathy and hazy cornea. This combination is atypical for classic Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch syndrome (WRS), where proptosis may occur but glaucoma and ectopia lentis are not characteristic features. The presence of both ectopia lentis and congenital glaucoma in a neonate with craniosynostosis and proptosis raises the possibility of a connective tissue or craniofacial disorder with secondary anterior segment dysgenesis. Differential considerations include a disorder of peroxisomal biogenesis (e.g., Zellweger spectrum), which can present with craniofacial anomalies, glaucoma, ectopia lentis, and hypotonia, but does not typically include lipodystrophy or polydactyly. Alternatively, a severe neonatal progeroid syndrome with expanded phenotype cannot be excluded. Additionally, high-resolution ocular ultrasound or anterior segment OCT would help document angle anatomy and lens position, and provide evidence for or against a primary developmental glaucoma versus secondary lens-related elevation.
